questions.question: How does file-based routing work in the App Router — segments, layouts vs templates, and the special files?
questions.title: App Router
questions.direct_answer: The app/ directory IS the route table: every folder is a URL segment; page.tsx makes the route public (no page = not routable), and layout.tsx wraps its subtree's pages and PERSISTS across navigations (the shell: nav, sidebar). Special files per segment: page.tsx (the route's UI + makes it addressable), layout.tsx (persistent wrapper — preserves state on navigation inside its subtree), template.tsx (same as layout but REMOUNTS per navigation — reset-state cases), loading.tsx (the Suspense fallback shown while the segment streams), error.tsx (the subtree's error boundary), not-found.tsx (the 404 UI), route.ts (an API route — endpoint instead of page). Dynamic: [id] matches one segment, [...slug] catches all, [[...slug]] optional; folders in (parens) = route groups (organize without affecting URL), _private = excluded from routing.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The route table, verified:

```text
app/
├── layout.tsx            ← ROOT layout (required: html+body) — persists for EVERYTHING
├── page.tsx               → /
├── blog/
│   ├── layout.tsx         ← blog shell — persists across /blog/* navigations
│   ├── page.tsx           → /blog
│   ├── loading.tsx        ← blog segment's Suspense fallback (instant nav feedback)
│   ├── [slug]/
│   │   └── page.tsx       → /blog/:slug (one dynamic segment)
│   └── (admin)/           ← route GROUP: folder invisible in the URL
│       └── posts/page.tsx → /blog/posts (no /admin/ in the path)
├── shop/[...slug]/
│   └── page.tsx          → /shop/a/b/c (catch-all: every remaining segment)
└── api/health/route.ts   → /api/health (endpoint, not a page)
```

The matching model (the interview core): navigation walks the FOLDERS from app/ down — the URL /blog/hello matches the chain layout(root) → layout(blog) → page([slug]=hello). Layouts wrap children as nested JSX-like slots; on navigation WITHIN the blog subtree, the blog layout does NOT re-render or remount — only the child page slot swaps (that's why nav state, scroll, and theme survive). A DIFFERENT subtree (leaving /blog for /shop) mounts shop's layouts fresh.

The three special files worth explaining precisely:
- loading.tsx: Next wraps the segment in <Suspense fallback={loading}> — the shell renders INSTANTLY and the page's data streams in (React streaming + the use of async Server Components). That's what makes App Router navigation feel fast by construction: no full-page white screen.
- error.tsx: a React error boundary scoped to the segment — a crash inside /blog/[slug] shows blog's error UI while the rest of the app stays alive; it must be a client component with reset().
- layout vs template (the question interviewers love): identical structure, ONE difference — template remounts its subtree (and itself) on every navigation, resetting state and re-running effects. Use it for per-page animations, page-view tracking, or forms that must reset per route. The default is layout; reach for template when reset-on-navigate is the DESIRED behavior.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    APP[app/ = the route table] --> SEG[folder = URL segment]
    SEG --> PAGE['page.tsx — makes the route addressable']
    SEG --> LAY['layout.tsx — PERSISTS across child navigations']
    SEG --> TPL['template.tsx — remounts per navigation (reset)']
    SEG --> LOAD['loading.tsx — Suspense fallback while segment streams']
    SEG --> ERR['error.tsx — segment error boundary']
    DYN['[id] one segment']  CA['[...slug] catch-all']  OCA['[[...slug]] optional']
    GRP['(group) — organize, invisible in URL']  PRV['_private — excluded']
    NAV[navigate within subtree] -.-> LAYP[layout does NOT remount — state survives]
    CROS[navigate to different subtree] -.-> FRESH[those layouts mount fresh]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why layouts persist (the mechanism under the DX): App Router navigation is NOT a page swap — the client router fetches the RSC payload for the new route, and React reconciles the tree: segments whose layouts are UNCHANGED keep their component instances (state, DOM, scroll anchors preserved), and only the changed segment's slots re-render. That's why app-level state in a root layout (auth context, theme provider) survives every navigation — it literally never unmounts. The cost of the same mechanism: layouts don't re-run effects per page (a surprise when you want per-page analytics — use template, or useEffect keyed on pathname in the client component).

The rendering-model layer beneath routing (what segments actually own): every segment is a RENDER BOUNDARY as well as a URL one — layouts can be static while their page streams, and each async component's Suspense position (where loading.tsx sits) is a streaming boundary. pushState navigation: the router serves an instant shell (cache/prefetch), loads the new segment tree, and React swaps the slots — prefetching (Link elements prefetch on viewport) is why subsequent navigations feel local. The URL→tree mapping composes: [id] hands params to the page (params.id — a Promise you await in v15+), and layouts never re-run for param changes in their subtree (dynamic params are below them) — page-level param reads only.

The vocabulary edges worth knowing (senior close): (a) route.ts replaces page.tsx semantics for non-UI (a segment has page XOR route); (b) parallel routes (@slot folders) render MULTIPLE pages in one layout via named slots — the dashboard-with-widgets architecture; (c) intercepting routes ((.)folder conventions) show a route MODALLY while its full page exists separately (the tweet-detail modal pattern); (d) Route Groups are the ONLY way to give two different paths the same URL shape with different layouts (a (marketing) and an (app) group can both root-layout differently). The one-liner: App Router is a folder tree = both a URL space and a Suspense/error/refresh boundary tree — one structure, three semantics.
